sections.h2: Ways to sell on the barrier island
sections.html:
Owners in Long Beach can go to market with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash purchase that comes with no repair requests. The barrier-island setting colors each choice, since Hurricane Sandy flooded the city in 2012, and condition and documentation carry real weight.

  • Agent listing: fits updated homes in strong blocks and sellers who can wait through a buyer's inspection and flood insurance quote.
  • For sale by owner: you run showings and negotiate, and your attorney prepares the contract and deed.
  • Cash buyer: suits a storm-worn bungalow, an inherited property or a rental you are done with, because the buyer takes it as-is.

Whatever you choose, gather your survey, any elevation certificate, insurance claim history and permit records first. Those papers answer the first questions every Long Beach buyer raises.

Long Beach is a dense oceanfront city on a barrier island, with the Atlantic to the south and Reynolds Channel to the north. It covers 2.22 square miles of land, less than a mile wide and about 3.5 miles long. Fewer than 40% of its homes are detached houses, so apartments, condos and attached homes make up much of the housing.

Neighborhoods vary a lot in feel and housing type:

  • West End: small bungalows and a few large houses on narrow streets that run from beach to bay.
  • East End: wider land between ocean and bay, with larger family houses.
  • The Canals and The Walks: canal-front streets and a network of narrow walkways between houses.
  • Central District and North Park: the area around City Hall and the Long Island Rail Road terminal.

Your neighborhood decides who is likely to buy. A West End bungalow, a canal-front house and an East End family home attract different buyers and different questions, so ask an agent for recent sales in your own neighborhood instead of a citywide number. Flood exposure also differs from block to block, and a buyer's insurance quote can change what they are willing to offer.

The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $696,400, and only 66.0% of homes are owner-occupied. The city has about 15,000 households. Gross rent is $2,515 at the midpoint.

The long commute fits the city's role as a commuter community. The Long Beach branch of the Long Island Rail Road ends at a terminal at Park Place and Park Avenue, and the city runs its own 24-hour bus service.

Monthly cost matters to buyers too. Mortgaged owners pay $3,519 a month at the midpoint, which limits what a buyer can spend on a house that needs a new roof or bulkhead.

sections.h2: Permits a buyer will ask about
sections.html:
Home work of many kinds needs a Building Department permit, and an unpermitted job in the house's past can slow a sale. The list covers roofs, siding, fences, driveways and curb cuts, central heating and air conditioning, sidewalks, bulkheads and docks, decks and porches, pools, hot tubs and saunas, fireplaces and chimneys, and all plumbing. Electrical work must be done by an electrician who holds a license, and a dumpster or roll-off container placed on the street needs a permit as well.

Additions, alterations and new structures also need approval, as does cutting a wall, removing a beam or changing a stairway or required exit. The department sits on the third floor of City Hall. Permit prices change, so ask the office for the current fee before you start work. If you did a bulkhead, deck or roof after Sandy, pull your permit and final inspection records now and keep them with your closing file.

Before you list, find out from the Building Department what it has on your address. A missing final inspection is cheaper to finish now than to explain once a buyer's attorney finds it.

sections.h2: How Long Beach taxes are billed and paid
sections.html:
One city office, the Tax Department, sends the bill for city real estate tax and residential sanitation and also collects the current-year Nassau County tax, so start there with most questions. You can pay on the third floor of City Hall with cash or a check, send payment to the City of Long Beach Treasurer at 1 West Chester Street, or pay online.

The City Charter lets properties with annual city taxes under $8,000 pay in two installments, while a bill of $8,000 or more is due in one payment in July. If your bill sits near that line, call the Tax Department to confirm whether you pay once or twice.

Escrow customers should watch for one trap: after a property moves into the single-payment group, a lender may keep collecting as though two installments still apply. Have your servicer review the escrow before closing, and request a written balance from the Tax Department for your attorney's closing adjustment.

If the City of Long Beach assesses your property, you appeal to the city's Board of Assessment Review. A filing with Nassau County's Assessment Review Commission does not preserve your rights there. The county's own filing window for its tentative roll runs from January 4 to March 1, 2027, with no fee and no extension, and it applies to county-assessed properties.

The commission can lower an assessment or leave it unchanged, nothing more. Ask the City of Long Beach assessor for the grievance dates and forms that apply to your parcel.

The state charges $2 for each $500 of price, rounded up, and sellers owe it unless the contract says otherwise. A residential price of $1 million or more brings a 1% mansion tax for the buyer. The TP-584 return and payment reach the county clerk within 15 days after the deed is delivered.

The Nassau County Clerk records deeds and lists recording fees on its real estate records pages. Ask your attorney or title company for the exact recording charge on your closing statement. After the sale, close your STAR registration.

With cash there is no buyer's lender or appraisal, the usual place a barrier-island deal stalls over flood insurance. A cash buyer still wants the survey, elevation certificate, claim history and permits. Weigh any offer against the net from a listing after commission, repairs and carrying costs, and let a New York attorney read the contract.

faqs.q: Does Nassau County assess my Long Beach house?
faqs.a: Not always. If the City of Long Beach assesses your property, you appeal to the city's own review board, and a filing with Nassau County's Assessment Review Commission does not cover that city assessment.

faqs.q: Who bills property tax in Long Beach?
faqs.a: The city's Tax Department bills City of Long Beach real estate tax and residential sanitation and also bills the current-year Nassau County tax. You can pay at City Hall, by mail to the City Treasurer or online.

faqs.q: Is my Long Beach city tax paid in one payment or two?
faqs.a: Properties with annual city taxes under $8,000 may pay in two installments, and $8,000 or more is due in one payment in July. Call the Tax Department if your bill is close to the line.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work on my Long Beach house?
faqs.a: Yes for most structural, mechanical and exterior work. Roofs, siding, fences, driveways, decks, pools, heating and cooling, plumbing and electrical work, and street dumpsters all need one.

faqs.q: Who pays transfer tax on a Long Beach sale?
faqs.a: The seller owes New York State's $2 per $500 transfer tax unless the contract shifts it, and the buyer owes the 1% mansion tax when a residential price is $1 million or more.
